catalog_citation: Nguyễn Văn Thắng (2007). Ambiguity of Identity: The Mieu in North Vietnam. Chiang Mai: Silkworm Books. ix+206 pp. [pp. 39-40, section 'From a monolingual to a trilingual people'; Appendix A 'Tones, consonants, and vowels of the Mieu language', p. 178]
catalog_locator: pp. 39-40 (ch. 2, section 'From a monolingual to a trilingual people'; preceding sentences: 'The Mieu language is characterized by its distinct syllable structure, tones, vowels, consonants, and sentence structure. It is monosyllabic.. Each syllable is made up of an initial consonant or consonant cluster, a vowel or diphthong, and a simultaneous tone.'); tone table repeated in Appendix A, p. 178 ('I. TONES: SYMBOL / TONE DESCRIPTION: None mid level; r high rising; x high falling; z mid rising; k low rising; s low falling; l falling with strong stop; v low falling ending with a glottal stop..'). IA scan prints the tone letter l as '1'.
catalog_quote: Mieu is also a tonal language, in which each syllable is pronounced with its own distinctive tone; a change in tone affects the meaning of a word. Mieu has eight tones characterized by voice quality and changes in pitch. These tones are symbolized by the writing system composed for the Hmong in Vietnam as follows: mid level (no symbol); high rising (r); high falling (x); mid rising (z); low rising (k); low falling (s); falling with a strong stop (l); and low falling with glottal stop or creaky voice at end (v) (appendix A).

new_statements.relation_note: Tonal, eight tones (pitch + phonation), monosyllabic; consonant and vowel inventories in Appendix A; Appendix B compares Mieu vocabulary with Hmong; no mention of stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Na Mieu (Na Meo) is a lexical-tone language: every (mostly monosyllabic) word/syllable carries one of eight tones distinguished by pitch contour and voice quality (mid level, high rising, high falling, mid rising, low rising, low falling, falling checked by a 'strong stop', low falling ending in glottal stop/creaky voice), written with the tone letters of the 1961 Vietnamese Hmong orthography (unmarked, r, x, z, k, s, l, v). Nothing is said about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the eight categories are presented via the Vietnamese Hmong writing system rather than from an instrumental or minimal-pair analysis of Mieu itself (Hsiu 2015's transcriptions of the Tuyên Quang variety show Chao values 55, 35, 53, 33, 22, 21, 13..)
new_statements.identity_note: The 'Mieu' / 'Na Mieu' of Cao Minh commune, Tràng Định district, Lạng Sơn (author's field site; also Thạch An/Cao Bằng, Na Rì/Bắc Kạn, Kim Quan/Tuyên Quang) = Vietnamese Na Miểu/Na Mẻo = Ethnologue/Glottolog Ná-Meo [neo], name1237; Glottolog itself files this book under name1237. sources.citation: Nguyễn Văn Lợi (2002). Vấn đề ngôn ngữ trong xác định thành phần dân tộc ở Việt Nam [The language question in determining ethnic composition in Vietnam]. Tạp chí Dân tộc học 2002, số 5: 50-57.
sources.note: Nothing on Na Mẻo tones or stress (the article does use tone evidence for Ngạn and Tống: 'các quá trình biến đổi thanh điệu', but not for Na Mẻo); it explicitly lists the Na Miểu group's language among 45 local-group languages of 21 ethnicities that still need linguistic investigation (2002).

sources.citation: Nguyễn Văn Thắng (2000). Nhận xét về bản sắc của người Miểu [Remarks on the identity of the Mieu]. Tạp chí Dân tộc học 2000, số 1: 85-95.
sources.note: No phonology content: only classification (Hmong dialect, 40/100 shared words with White Hmong), the shift from monolingual to trilingual (Mieu/Tày/Việt) since 1956, and language maintenance attitudes.
